title: Reporting a Lost Bag at the Station
context: A passenger reports a bag left on a train and is told how lost property is handled.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Lost property, good afternoon.

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: Hello — I think I've left a bag on a train. I only realised when I got to the office.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Oh dear, that's always a nuisance. Don't worry, it happens more often than you'd imagine, and we get quite a lot of it back — let's see if we can track yours down.

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: Thank you, I was hoping you'd say that. I only noticed when I reached for my badge at the office door, and by then the train was long gone.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: We'll see what we can do. Which service were you on?

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: The 8:14 from Ashford, arriving here at about twenty to nine.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Right, that's the Ashford service that terminates on platform six. Was the bag with you in the carriage or in the rack at the end?

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: In the overhead rack, above my seat. Coach C, I think, near the doors.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: That helps. Can you describe it?

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: It's a soft rucksack, dark green, with a broken zip on the front pocket. It's got a luggage tag with my initials on it — J.M.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Dark green rucksack, broken front zip, tag with initials. Anything distinctive inside?

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: A grey laptop, a notebook, and a pair of running shoes. Oh — and a blue umbrella strapped to the side.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: That's a good, clear description. The combination of the laptop and the umbrella should make it easy to spot among the other bags.

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: I hope so. The laptop's the main worry, if I'm honest.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Good, the umbrella is the sort of detail that identifies it. Now, your name and a contact number?

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: Jenna Marsh. My mobile is 0-7-7-0-0, then 9-1-4-2-6-3.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: 07700 914263. And an email in case we can't reach you by phone?

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: It's j dot marsh at brightwell dot co dot uk.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Perfect, that's everything I need from you for now.

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: Thanks. Do you know roughly how long all this usually takes?

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Thank you. Now, what happens next. Anything found on a terminating train is collected by the cleaning team and brought to the depot, not to this office, and the depot sends items across the following morning. So if it was handed in today, we'd see it tomorrow.

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: So there's no point coming in this evening.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: None at all, I'm afraid. What I'd suggest is that you check the online register first. Every item is logged with a reference number, and you can search by station and date. Save yourself the journey.

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: That's useful. Do I need some sort of reference number to search it, or can anyone look?

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Anyone can look. You just search by the station and roughly when you travelled, and any matching items come up with a photo.

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: How long do you keep things?

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Three months for most items. Electronic items we keep for six months, because people so often come back for them late. After that they go to auction, and the proceeds go to a railway charity.

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: That makes sense. I suppose laptops and phones go missing more often than most things, then?

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: They're certainly the ones people chase hardest, yes. With a phone or a laptop, people will ring us nearly every day until it turns up, whereas a hat or a scarf, people often just let go.

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: Is there a fee?

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: There's a handling charge of five pounds for a bag, and it's ten pounds for anything with a laptop in it, because those are stored separately in a secure cabinet. Cash or card, either is fine.

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: That's reasonable. And if it turns up somewhere else?

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Everything is on the same national register, so if a colleague at another station logs a dark green rucksack, your description will match it and we'll contact you. That happens more often than you'd think — people pick up the wrong bag and hand it in three stops down the line.

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: That's reassuring, actually. I'd assumed that once it was gone, it was gone.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Not at all. We really do reunite most bags with their owners eventually — it's usually just a case of being patient.

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: Thank you, that's very helpful.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: Give it until midday tomorrow and then check the register. If nothing shows by Friday, call us back and we'll widen the search.

script.speaker: Passenger
script.text: Will do. Thanks again for your help, I really do appreciate it.

script.speaker: Clerk
script.text: You're very welcome. I hope it turns up quickly, and try not to worry too much in the meantime.

questions.instruction: Complete the lost property form below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.explanation: “Jenna Marsh.” The surname is what the form line is missing, and it is repeated in her email address.
“The 8:14 from Ashford, arriving here at about twenty to nine.” The arrival time is the distractor.

questions.sentence: Bag left in the overhead rack in coach ___.
questions.explanation: “In the overhead rack, above my seat. Coach C, I think, near the doors.” Platform six is a different number in the same passage.

questions.sentence: Item: a dark green ___ with a broken front zip.
questions.explanation: “It's a soft rucksack, dark green, with a broken zip on the front pocket.” The clerk repeats the description back.

questions.sentence: Attached to the side: a blue ___.
questions.explanation: “And a blue umbrella strapped to the side.” The clerk singles it out as the identifying detail.
She reads it in groups — “9-1-4-2-6-3” — and the clerk reads the whole number back as 07700 914263.

questions.instruction: Answer the questions below. Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.question: Where are items from a terminating train taken first?
questions.explanation: “Anything found on a terminating train is collected by the cleaning team and brought to the depot, not to this office.”

questions.question: What does the clerk suggest checking before travelling in?
questions.explanation: “What I'd suggest is that you check the online register first… Save yourself the journey.”

questions.question: For how many months are electronic items kept?
questions.explanation: “Three months for most items. Electronic items we keep for six months.” Three months is the general rule and the distractor.

questions.question: What is the handling charge for a bag containing a laptop?
questions.explanation: “There's a handling charge of five pounds for a bag, and it's ten pounds for anything with a laptop in it.” Five pounds applies to a bag without one.
